la:adv:profecto.gloss: actually, indeed, really, truly, surely, assuredly, of course
senses: actually, indeed, really, truly, surely, assuredly, of course
la:adv:profecto.html:
prŏfectō, adv.
pro-facto
, a particle of affirmation, confirmation, and declaration,
actually, indeed, really, truly, surely, assuredly, by all means, certainly, etc. (very freq. and class.): neque di regunt neque profecto deūm summus rex omnibus curat, Att. ap. (Trag. Rel v 142 Rib.): profecto edepol,: profecto, ut loquor, res ita est,: non est ita, judices, non est profecto,: retorquet oculos profecto,: profecto negare non potes,: nunc quidem profecto Romae es,: si modo di sunt, ut profecto sunt,: meministi enim profecto,; ; ; cf. ; ; ; ; ; Liv 1, 15; 44, 2; 54, 1.—Strengthened by other particles; profecto hercle,: vere enim profecto,

la:verb:profugio.gloss: to flee, run away or escape
senses: to flee, run away or escape
la:verb:profugio.html:
prŏ-fŭgĭo (with first syll. long, ), fūgi, 3, v. a. and n.
Act., to flee before or from, to flee, fly from any thing (poet. and post-Aug.): Phocaeorum Velut profugit execrata civitas Agros,: conspectum conversationemque civium suorum profugit, (36), 4: sedes suas,: natos,: dominos,; .—
Neutr., to flee, run away, escape (class.): domo profugiens,: pedibus Hadrumetum profugerat,: Babyloniam,: Cirtam,; : aliquo,: longius,: istinc,: ex oppido,: in Britanniam,: domo,; : cum vi prope justorum armorum profugisset, B. and K. (Klotz, vim): in exsilium,: ex proelio in provinciam,: e carcere,; .—
In partic., to flee for succor to one, take refuge with one (class.): se profugere ad Brutum,: ad Ciceronem,; ; .

la:noun:profectio.html:
prŏfectĭo, ōnis, f.
id.
.
Lit., a going away, setting out, departure (class.): profectione laeti, Pac. ap. : profectio et reversio alicujus,: profectionem parare, to prepare for setting out, Caes B. C. 1, 27. Cethegi profectio in Hispaniam, ; ; Liv 2, 14; 38, 59.—
Transf., of things, the source whence any thing is obtained: profectio ipsius pecuniae requiratur,.

la:verb:proficio.gloss: to advance, make progress, make headway
senses: to advance, make progress, make headway
la:verb:proficio.html:
prōfĭcĭo, fēci, fectum, 3,
v. n and a. [pro-facio], to go forward, advance, gain ground, make progress.
Lit. (very rare): cum quinqueremis sola non proficeret,.—
Trop., to go on, advance, make progress; to profit, derive advantage; to perform, effect, accomplish, obtain, etc. (class.; cf. procedo).
Of persons: si nihil in oppugnatione oppidi profecisset,: ubi diligentiā nostrorum nihil his rebus profici posse intellexerunt,: plus multitudine telorum,: loci opportunitate,: antesignani tantum profecere, ut pellerent omnes,: multum profecit,: si modo in philosophiā aliquid profecimus, have made any progress, Cic.

Off. 3, 8, 37: ea,—Of the sick, to get better: si quidquam profecerint, Cael. Aur Acut. 2, 10, 71 proficiens aegrotus,—

Of manim subjects, to grow, increase (mostly post-Aug.): id (vitis genus) quod umore proficit,: proficiente pretio,rising,.—In pass.: sed etiam ad summam profectum aliquid puto,: postquam nihil proficiebatur,.—In a bad sense: proficere in pejus,to become worse and worse,.—
In partic., to be useful, serviceable, advantageous, etc., to effect, accomplish; to help, tend, contribute, conduce (class.; cf. prosum) ea suo quaeque loco, ubi plurimum proficere et valere possent, collocabat,: nulla res tantum ad dicendum proficit, quantum scriptio,; Liv 3, 61: profectura aliquid tum tua verba puta, Ov P. 3, 1, 138: aut nihil in melius tot rerum proficit usus?.—Of remedies: radice vel herbā Proficiente nihil,; nec alia res celerius proficit, is of service, Plin 27, 11, 72, § 96: axungia proficit ad strumas,; pirorum ligni cinis contra fungos efficacius proficit,: radix anethi vel in febribus proficit,.—Impers.: multum proficiet illud demonstrare, quemadmodum scripsisset,.—Hence, prōfĭcĭenter, adv., successfully (eccl. Lat.), Aug Ep. 80: incedere, Hil. Trin. 1, 22; Cassiod in Psa. 133, 2.

la:noun:profectus.gloss: advance, progress, effect, increase, growth, profit, success
senses: advance, progress, effect, increase, growth, profit, success
la:noun:profectus.html:
prōfectus (with the first syllable short, Aus. ldyll. 4, 70), ūs, m.
proficio
,
advance, progress, effect, increase, growth, profit, success (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): sine profectu, Ov M. 9, 50: verbaque profectu dissimulata carent,; ; ; ; ; : in quo quantum esset ingenii, quantum etiam profectus, sermo primus ostendit,progress,: experimentum profectus tui capere animi firmitate,: donec blandlente profectu prodire in scenam concupiit,: puer magni profectus in eā arte obiit,.—So, the improvement,convalescence of the sick, .—In plur.: in similitudine et temporum et profectuum,.

la:verb:proficiscor.html:
prŏfĭciscor, fectus, 3,
v. dep. n. [profacio, facesso, faciscor; orig., to make, i. e. put one's self forward; hence], to set out, start, go, march, travel, depart, etc. (class.; cf. progredior).
Lit.: proficisci ad dormiendum,to go to sleep,: ad somnum,: ad sedes inquirendas,: pabulatum frumentatumque,: subsidio alicui,: ad bellum,; ; : ad eam domum,: Puteolos,: in Illyricum,: in pugnam,: in bellum,; : in expeditionem,: in Volscos,; ; : in exercitum,: hinc in pistrinum rectā viā,: contra quosdam barbaros, Nep Eum 3, 5: Cyprum,: Corinthum,: domum,: Genabum,: Romam,: domos,: Circeios,: jussit proficisci exilium quovis gentium, Att. ap. (Trag. Rel. v 599 Rib.): Jovinus eadem loca profectus, Amm 27, 8, 2.—With supine: porro proficiscor quaesitum,.—Absol.: proficisci,to make a journey,: ab urbe,to set out, depart,: ab Antio,: ex castris,to break up,: e castris,: domo,; ; : portu,: regno,: Athenis,: de Formiano,.—
Transf., to be going or about to go, to intend to go to a place, to start (ante-class.): potin' ut me ire, quo profectus sum, sinas?: tu profectus alio fueras, Ter Eun. 2, 2, 49: cum proficisceretur,; ; ; .—
Trop.
In gen., to go, come, proceed: nunc proficiscemur ad reliqua,.—
In partic.
To set out, begin, commence: ut inde oratio mea proficiscatur, unde, etc.,: cum omnis haec quaestio ab eo proficiscatur,; a philosophiā profectus Xenophon scripsit historiam,: ei proficiscendum est ab omni mundo,.—
To come forth, spring, arise, proceed, originate: cum omnia officia a principiis naturae proficiscantur, ab iisdem necesse est proficisci ipsam sapientiam,; ; : falsis initiis profecta,: ex medicinā nihil oportet putare proficisci, nisi quod ad corporis utilitatem spectet,: quaecumque a me ornamenta ad te proficiscentur, shall pass from me to you, i. e. you shall receive from me, : omnia quae a me profecta sunt in te, tibi accidisse gratissime, all you have received from me, : ut plura a parente proficisci non potuerint,: qui a Zenone profecti sunt,who have proceeded from him, his disciples,; cf.: omnes ab Aristotele profecti,.—So, to express descent (poet.): Tyriā de gente profecti,; .—Act. collat. form prŏfĭcisco, ĕre, to set out, go, etc. (anteclass.): priusquam proficisco,; hortatur hominem, quam primum proficisceret, Turp. ap. .

senses: to make known, produce in public, publish, reveal
la:verb:profero.html:
prō-fĕro, tŭli, lātum, ferre (
inf. pass. parag. proferrier, ; proferis for profers,), v. a.
Lit.
To carry or bring out, to bring forth (class.; cf.: prodo, produco, adduco): Al. Vin' proferri pateram? Am. Proferri volo. Al. Fiat: tu, Thessala, intus pateram proferto foras,: arma tormentaque ex oppido,: (nummos) ex arcā,.—
To extend, stretch, or thrust out: linguam in tussiendo,: manum,: digitum,.—
Se proferre, to raise one's self, show one's self, appear (post-Aug.): draco e pulvino se proferens,.—
To offer, proffer: alicui minas viginti argenti,.—Esp.,
Proferre gradum or pedem, to go on, proceed: gradum proferam, progredi properabo,: gradum pedum proferre, Enn ap : passus, Lucr 4, 874: longe pedem,; cf.: pedem, Hor A. P 135. —
As milit. t. t.: signa proferre, to advance the standards, march on, Liv 4, 32, 10; so, proferre inde castra,: quidquid ab urbe longius proferrent arma,.—Also,
Nautical t t.: pedibus profatis in contrarium navigare,to sail close to the wind,; cf.: prolato pede transversos captare notos,.—
Transf.
To bring forth, produce, cause to grow, of plants (postAug.): caelum laurum patitur, atque etiam nitidissimam profert,: semen, (al. perfert). —
Of pronunciation, to utter, pronounce (post-Aug.): extremas syllabas,.—
To extend, enlarge (class.): castra, Caes, B. C. 1, 81: et proferre libet fines,: pomoerium,.—
To put off, defer, adjourn, etc. (class.): rem aliquot dies, Cat. ap. : auctionis diem laxius proferre,: aliquid in diem posterum,; cf. .—
Of a painter, to bring out, to represent distinctly (post-Aug.); venas protulit,.—
Trop.
With se, to raise, elevate one's self (post-Aug.): qui se ipsi protulerunt,who have raised themselves from ignorance,; .—
To bring out, make known, produce in public, publish (class.): ejus (orationis) proferendae arbitrium tuum,: artem,to exhibit publicly,—
To bring forth, produce, invent, discover, make known, reveal (class.): artem,: palam proferre aliquid, Ter Ad. 3, 2, 41: cum illa indicia communis exitii indagavi, patefeci, protuli,: aliquid foras,: rem in medium,: secreta animi,: Montanum, quia protulerit ingenium, extorrem agi,displayed his genius,—
To bring forward, quote, cite, mention (class.); libros,: testes, legatos,: auctores,: nominatim multos,; paucos belli duces praestantissimos,: vinolentiam alicujus,: vim, potentiam, factiones, divitias, clientelas, affinitates adversariorum,: aliquid in medium,; ; : memoriter Progeniem suam usque ab avo atque atavo, Ter Phorm. 2, 3, 48: exempla omnium nota,.—
To extend, enlarge: fines officiorum,: memoriam alicujus,to prolong,: ut vita ejus debuerit inmortalitate proferri,; 3, 7, 14.—
To impel: si paulo longius pietas Caecilium protulisset,.—With se: cum se ad clarissimorum civium strages caedesque proferret,.—
To lengthen out, prolong (class.): beatam vitam usque ad rogum proferre,: ut depositi proferret fata parentis,.

la:noun:professio.html:
prŏfessĭo, ōnis, f.
profiteor
,
a public acknowledgment, declaration, expression, profession, promise (mostly post-Aug.).
In gen.: professio bonae voluntatis, Planc. ap. : Canidius timidius decessit, quam professioni ejus congruebat,: memores professionis, of our promise (of brevity), : aperta,: suae opinionis,expression,: summa stultitiae,: flagitii,: pietatis,.—
Transf., a sign, token (post-class.): vitiorum,.—
In partic., a public declaration or specification of one's person, name, property, business, etc. (class.): IS. APVD. QVEM. EA. PROFESSIO FIET, etc., Tab. Her. in Haubold, Mon. Leg. p. 101 sq.; : tu vero confice professionem, si potes. Etsi haec pecunia ex eo genere est, ut professione non egeat,: post professionem de fideicommisso factam,; ; .—
Transf.
A public register of persons or property thus given in (class.): in Leontino jugerum subscriptio ac professio non est plus triginta millium,.—
A business or profession which one publicly avows (class.): professio bene dicendi,: grammaticae,: sapientiae,: magicae artis,: professionem honestarum artium malis corruperant moribus,: ista salutaris, the art of healing, medicine, Cels. praef.: ultimae professionis homines, i. e. vilissimi artificii,; Dig 2, 13, 9.

la:verb:profiteor.gloss: to declare publicly, own (up to) or confess openly, acknowledge, avow, profess
senses: to declare publicly, own (up to) or confess openly, acknowledge, avow, profess
to profess, claim; to declare oneself (as), practice (as)
to make a show of, show, display
to make a public statement or a return of
to be a teacher or professor
la:verb:profiteor.html:
prŏfĭtĕor, fessus,
v (old form of the inf. PROFITEREI, and of the imper. PROFITEMINO, several times in the Tab. Her, in Haubold, Mon. Leg. p. 99 sq.), v. dep. a. [pro-fateor], to declare publicly, to own freely, to acknowledge, avow, confess openly, profess (class.).
In gen.
Absol.: neque vis tuā voluntate ipse profiteri,: ita libenter confitetur, ut non solum fateri, sed etiam profiteri videatur,: fateor atque etiam profiteor et prae me fero,.—
With acc.: profiteri et in medium proferre aliquid,: cur ea non profitenda putabas?.—
With obj. clause: profitentur Carnutes, se nullum periculum recusare,; .—
With de: de parricidio professum,: de semet professo,.—
In partic.
Profiteri se aliquem, to declare one's self or profess to be something: profiteri se grammaticum,; Poët. ap. ; profiteri se patrem infantis,: se legatum,: se candidatum consulatūs,: professus amicum,.—With esse: triduo me jure consultum esse profitebor,: me omnium provinciarum defensorem esse profitebor,.—
Profiteri aliquid, to profess an art, science, etc.: profiteri philosophiam,to declare one's self a philosopher,; medicinam, to profess medicine, to practise as a physician, Cels. praef.; ; jus,.—In pass.: rem non professam apud nos tenemus,. —Absol.: profiteri, to be a teacher or professor (post-Aug.): cum omnes qui profitentur, audiero,: translatus est in Siciliam, ubi nunc profitetur,.—
Profiteri indicium, to give evidence, make a deposition against accomplices: multis hortantibus indicium profitetur,; , ; : summum supplicium decernebatur, ni professus indicium foret,.—
To offer freely, propose voluntarily, to promise: quis profitetur? who volunteers? Plaut Capt. 3, 1, 20: se ad eam rem adjutorem,: ego vero tibi profiteor atque polliceor eximium et singulare meum studium in omni genere officii,: si vos in eam rem operam vestram profitemini,: Varro profitetur se alterā die ad colloquium venturum,: sumunt gentiles arma professa manus,arms that promise a combat,: magna, Hor A. P. 14; : grandia,.—
To disclose, show, display, make a show of; dolorem, : sola Jovem Semele vidit Jovis ora professum,: vitate viros cultum formamque professos,.—
To make a public statement or return of any thing (as of one's name, property, business, etc.): censum (one's estate),; Tab. Her. in Haubold, Mon. Leg. p. 99 sq. (q. v.): ut aratores jugera sationum suarum profiterentur,: apud decemviros, quantum habeat praedae,: greges ovium ad publicanum,: frumentum, Liv 4, 12: furtum,: rem alienam,: rem apud publicanum,; .—Absol.: ne decipiat (publicanus) profiteri volentes,; and 5: nomen,to give in one's name, announce one's self,; also without nomen: Catilina prohibitus erat petere consulatum, quod intra legitimos dies profiteri nequiverit,: nam et quaesturam petentes, quos indignos judicavit, profiteri vetuit,: professae (sc. feminae), i. e. common prostitutes, who had to give in their names to the aedile, .—Trop.: in his nomen suum profitetur,among these he reckons himself,.—Hence, prŏ-fessus, a, um, P. a., in passive signif., known, manifest, confessed (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): culpa professa,: dux,.—Ex or de professo, openly, avowedly, intentionally, professedly: non ex professo eam (potentiam) non petere,: vir ex professo mollis, Macr S. 2, 9.—De professo (postclass.): ac ne id quidem de professo audet,openly,.

la:verb:professus.gloss: having confessed, acknowledged, avowed, professed, declared
senses: having confessed, acknowledged, avowed, professed, declared
taken in the passive voice: declared

la:verb:profligo.gloss: to strike or dash to the ground
senses: to strike or dash to the ground
to finish, conclude, resolve, put an end to
la:verb:profligo.html:
prō-flīgo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.,
to strike or dash to the ground, to cast down utterly, overthrow, overcome, conquer (class.; syn.: sterno, prosterno).
Lit.: inimicos profligare,: copias hostium,: classem hostium,: hostes,: proelia,i. e. the warriors,: aciem virorum,; .—
Trop.
To overthrow, ruin, destroy: rem publicam,: tantas opes,: undique se suosque profligante fortunā,: valetudinem,.—
To overwhelm, crush in spirit: quanti illum maerore afflictum esse et profligatum putatis,.—
To bring almost to an end, to almost finish, despatch: bellum commissum ac profligatum conficere,: profligato fere Samnitium bello,; : profligatum bellum ac paene sublatum,: profligata jam haec, et paene ad exitum adducta quaestio est,: omnia ad perniciem profligata,: sperans, ante Vitellii adventum profligari plurimum posse,that it would be brought nearly to an end,: profligaverat bellum Judaicum Vespasianus,; Flor 2, 15, 2; ; : profligatis in Africā rebus,: victoriam,: quantum profligatum sit,how far advanced,; cf. .—Hence, prōflīgātus, a, um, P. a.
Wretched, miserable, vile (class.; syn. perditus): senatoria judicia perdita profligataque,.—
In a moral sense, corrupt, dissolute, abandoned, profligate (class.): tu omnium mortalium profligatissime ac perditissime,: homines,: omnia ad perniciem profligata atque perdita,: profligatissimus quisque,.—
Of time, advanced (post-Aug.): profligatae aetatis (homo), (al. Vit. Beat. 29, 2).—In neutr. absol.: in profligato esse,to be almost ended,.

la:adj:profugus.gloss: that which flees, has fled, fugitive
senses: that which flees, has fled, fugitive
la:adj:profugus.html:
prŏfŭgus, a, um, adj.
profugio
,
that flees or has fled, fugitive (not in Cic. or Cæs.; cf. fugitivus).
In gen.: profugus domo,: ex urbe,: ex Peloponneso,: e proelio,: a proelio,: ad rebelles,.—Of animals: boves profugae,: juvenci,: taurus profugus altaribus,; cf. currus,.—With gen.: Tiridates regni profugus,: bis vinculorum (Hannibalis) profugus,escaped from,.—
Transf., fleeing hither and thither, vagabond, roving, wandering, unsettled (poet.): profugi Scythae,: Scythes,; .—
In partic., that flees from his native country, fugitive, banished, exiled: Hannibal patriā profugus,: Trojani, qui profugi incertis sedibus vagabantur,: fato profugus,: classis,.—
Subst.: prŏ-fŭgus, i, and prŏfŭga, ae, m.
A fugitive, banished person, exile (poet.): profugus patriam deseras,: profugo affer opem,; : servi alieni profugae,; cf. P.—
An apostate: reus suae religionis aut profugus,.

la:adj:profundus.html:
prŏ-fundus, a, um, adj.,
deep, profound, vast (class.; syn. altus).
Lit.: mare profundum et immensum,; : per inane profundum,: pontus,: Acheron,: Danubius,: fornax,: valles,: terrae foramen,: atque hiavit humus multa, vasta, et profunda, Dietsch: vulnera,.—Sup.: profundissimus libidinum gurges,.—
Subst.: prŏfundum, i, n., depth.
In gen.: esse in profundo (aquae),

4, 23, 64: maris,; : immensa ac profunda camporum,.—

In partic.
The depths of the sea, the deep, the sea (class.): ex profundo molem ad caelum erigit, Att. ap. : jecissem ipse me potius in profundum, ut ceteros conservarem, quam, etc.,: profundo Vela dabit,: vastum,; : summum,: indomitum,: pater ipse profundi,i.e. Neptune,: genitor profundi,: Pamphylium,: profundi imperium,; ; ; ; .—
In comic. lang., an abyss, meaning the stomach, in a lusus verbb. with fundus, .—
Transf.
Thick, dense (poet. and in post - class. prose): Erebi nox,: silvae,; : ursi villis profundioribus,.—
Like altus, high (poet.): caelum profundum,: caelum,; ; : altitudo,; .—
Subst.: prŏfundum, i, n., height: altum caeli,.—
In a great quantity, copious, unlimited, without stint (poet.): merum,.—
Of the underworld, infernal (poet.): Manes,: Chaos,: Juppiter, i. e. Pluto,: Juno, = Proserpina,.—
Trop.
Deep, bottomless, profound, boundless, immoderate (class.): profundae libidines,: avaritia,: cupido imperii et divitiarum,: vitia animi,: cupiditas confundendi omnia,: securitas,: otium,: profundissimā pace florere (=summā),: caedes,: tempestas,: gula,: venter,: immensusque ruit profundo Pindarus ore,i.e. with inexhaustible copiousness of expression,: scientia,: cum me somnus profundus in imum barathrum demergit,: in profundam ruinam cupidinis se praecipitare,, p. 202, 1.—
Deep, obscure, unknown (post-Aug.): in profundo esse,to be unknown,.—
Subst.: prŏfun-dum, i, n., a depth, abyss (class.): in profundo veritatem penitus abstrudere,: Democritus (dixit) in profundo veritatem esse demersam,: in profundum ultimarum miseriarum abjectus,: immergere aliquem miserabiliter profundo cladium,, ext. 7: in profundum injuriarum et turpitudinis decidere,, ext. 2; cf.: de profundis clamavi ad te,.—Hence, adv.: prŏfun-dē, deeply (post-Aug.): in bibendo profundius nares mergere,; .

la:verb:profor.html:
prŏ-for, fātus, 1 (
inf. profarier, Prud. στεφ. 10, 939), v. dep. a., to say or speak out, to say, speak (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose).
In gen.: veteres Casmenas cascam rem volo profari, tell, relate, Att. ap. Müll.: quod jam et mehe Piget paternum nomen, maternum pudet Profari, Pac. ap. (Trag. Rel. v. 145 Rib.): pudor prohibebat plura profari,: tum breviter Dido, vultum demissa, profatur,: et sic accensa profatur,: quibus ille profatur: Forsitan, etc.,: vera profari,: sic ille profatus,: clamore magno,.—
In partic., to foretell, predict, prophesy: quando dies adveniet, quem profata Morta est, Liv. And. ap. (acc. to Hom. Odyss. 2, 99): Pythia quae tripodi a Phoebi lauroque profatur,; : Delio profante,; . —Hence, prŏfātum. i, n., a statement, proposition, axiom (post-class.): ἀξιώματα, quae M. Varro alias profata, alias proloquia appellat, .

la:verb:profundo.html:
prō^-fundo, fūdi, fūsum, 3, v. a.,
to pour out or forth, to shed copiously, to cause to flow (class.).
Lit.: sanguinem suum profundere omnem cupit, dummodo profusum hujus ante videat,: sanguinem pro patriā,; : vim lacrimarum,: lacrimas oculis,; ; ; : sanguinem ex oculis,: aquam,: vinum,: vina deo tamquam sitienti,; : aquas sub mensas,. —With se, to burst or gush forth: lacrimae se subito profuderunt,.—
Transf.
To stretch at full length, to prostrate (poet.): cum somnus membra profudit,: praecipites profusae in terram,.—Mid.: profusus, abjectus jacens. Pacuvius: profusus gemitu, murmure, stretched at full length, Paul. ex Müll. (Trag. Rel. v. 321 Rib.). —
To pour or cast out, bring forth, produce (class.): posticā parte profudit, Lucil. ap. : (puerum) ex alvo matris natura profudit,: sonitus,: ignes,: omnia ex ore,: pectore voces,to pour forth, utter,: vocem,: clamorem,; : voces,: vitia,: dolorem,: palmites,.—
With se, to pour forth, rush forth or out; of bees: cum se nova profundent examina,; of archers: omnis multitudo sagittariorum se profudit,; of luxuriant plants: ea, quae se nimium profuderunt,have shot out, sent out shoots,: profundit se supra modum numerus palmitum,.—
Trop., to cast or throw away: ventis verba profundere,: quae si non profundere ac perdere videbor,.—
In partic.
To throw away.
In a bad sense, spend uselessly; to lavish, dissipate, squander: profundat, perdat, pereat,; : patrimonia,: pecunias in res,.—
In a good sense, to spend, sacrifice: non modo pecuniam, sed vitam etiam profundere pro patriā,.—
Esp., of life, to yield, give up: animam,: si pateretur natura, vel denas animas profundere praestabat in pugnā, quam, etc.,: spiritum in acie,.—
To pour out, vent; to expend, exert, employ; to set forth, show, explain: odium in aliquem,: omnes profudi vires animi atque ingenii mei,: res universas,to set forth, explain,.—
With se, to pour itself forth, i. e. to rush forth, break out: voluptates cum inclusae diutius, subito se nonnumquam profundunt atque eiciunt universae,: si totum se ille in me profudisset,had wholly poured himself out to me, had been liberal,: in questus flebiles sese in vestibulo curiae profuderunt,.—Hence, prŏ-fūsus, a, um, P. a.
Lit., spread out, extended, hanging down (ante- and postclass.): cauda profusa usque ad calces,.—Comp.: equi coma et cauda profusior,longer,.—
Trop.
Lavish, extravagant, profuse (class.; cf. prodigus): perditus ac profusus nepos,: reus,.—With gen.: alieni appetens, sui profusus,lavish of his own,.—With in and abl.: simul ad jacturam temporis ventum est, profusissimi in eo, cujus unius honesta avaritia est,.—Of things abstr. and concr.: profusis sumptibus vivere,: profusa luxuria in aedificiis,.—
In a good sense, liberal (poet.): mens profusa,: homo,.—
Costly, expensive: amare profusas epulas,: convivia,.—
Immoderate, excessive, extravagant: profusa hilaritas,: genus jocandi,: cupido,.—Sup.: profusissima libido,.—Adv.: prŏfūsē.
Lit., lavishly, extravagantly, profusely (post-Aug.): aedes profuse exstructa,at an immoderate expense,.—Sup.: festos et solemnes dies profusissime celebrabat,.—
Trop.
In disorder, confusedly: consul obstitit profuse tendentibus suis in castra,.—
Immoderately, excessively: profuse prolixeque laudare,.—Comp.: eo profusius sumptui deditus erat,.

la:adj:profanus.html:
prŏfānus, a, um, adj.
pro - fanum; prop. before the temple, i. e. outside of it; hence, opp. to the temple as a sacred object
,
unholy, not sacred, common, profane.
Lit.: profanum quod non est sacrum, Plautus: Sacrum an profanum habeas parvi penditur, Paul. ex Müll.; cf.: profanum est, quod fani religione non tenetur, ib.: Trebatius profanum id proprie dici ait, quod ex religioso vel sacro

in hominum usum proprietatem conversum est, : loci consecrati an profani,; opp. sacrum, cum omnia illā victoriā suā profana fecisset, : res profanae et usu pollutae,: flamma,: usus,.—Of persons: procul o, procul este, profani, Conclamat vates, ye uninitiated, Verg A. 6, 258: Cereris ritus vulgare profanis, Ov A. A. 2, 601 profanum vulgus,: vulgus, Gell. N A. praef. fin.—

Transf.
Wicked, impious (poet.): mens profana, Ov M 2, 833: verba,: odia,: profanus Phorbas, Ov M. 11, 413 sit spes fallendi, miscebis sacra profanis, Hor Ep. 1, 16, 54.— Subst.prŏfānum, i, n., wickedness, impiety (post-Aug.): civilium bellorum profano,.—
Unlearned, ignorant (post-class.); with gen.: litterarum profani (opp.: doctrina initiati),; : qui profani sunt a sacramento veritatis,strangers to,: a veritate,; .—
Ill-boding (poet.): profanus bubo, Ov M 6, 431 avis,.— Hence, adv.: prŏfānē, wickedly, profanely (post-class.); illudere,: de divinitate disputare,.

senses: to flow or run forth or along; discharge
to flow or spring forth, issue, proceed
la:verb:profluo.html:
prō-flŭo, xi, xum, 3, v. n.,
to flow forth or along (class.).
Lit.: Mosa profluit ex monte Vogeso,: si lacrimae ab oculis et pituita a naribus profluent,: umor profluit,: sanguis profluens, Enn. ap. : sudor,: per fossas,: ad mare,.—
Transf.
To cause a running or flow: gravedo profluit,.—
To be relaxed: videndum est an adstrictum corpus sit, an profluat,: si venter profluit,.—
Trop., to flow forth, issue, proceed (class.): quae ab hoc fonte profluant, Müll.: cujus ore sermo melle dulcior profluebat,: equidem ab his fontibus profluxi ad hominum famam,: ad incognitas artes, to proceed to, to fall or hit upon, .— Hence, prōflŭens, entis, P. a., flowing along (class.).
Lit.: aqua profluens,.—
Subst.: prōflŭens, entis, f. (sc. aqua), running water (class.): in profluentem deferri,; cf. ; ; .—
Trop., of speech, flowing, fluent: genus sermonis affert non liquidum, non fusum ac profluens, sed exile, aridum, concisum,: profluens et perennis loquacitas,: profluens atque expedita celeritas,: profluens quiddam habuit Carbo et canorum,: eloquentia,.—Sup.: manuum suarum profluentissima largitas,.— Hence, adv.: prōflŭenter, flowingly; trop., easily (class.): ergo omnia profluenter, absolute, prospere,. —Comp., of speech, more fluently (postclass.): profluentius exsequi,.
